A.explanation: This would result from cubing the diameter ratio instead of squaring it for area. Cross-sectional area depends on $d^2$, not $d^3$.

B.explanation: This is the inverse of the area ratio $A_P/A_Q$ alone. It omits the factor of 2 from the larger resistivity of wire Q.

D.explanation: This inverts the required ratio. Wire P needs a shorter length because wire Q has larger area despite its larger resistivity.

hints: Notice the two wires have equal resistance $R = \rho L/A$, with $\rho_Q = 2\rho_P$.
Connect diameter to area: since $A = \pi d^2/4$, doubling diameter makes the area of Q four times the area of P.
Set $R_P = R_Q$ and rearrange to $L_P/L_Q = (\rho_Q/\rho_P)(A_P/A_Q)$, then substitute the two ratios.
walkthrough: Write the resistance formula for each wire: $R_P = \rho_P L_P/A_P$ and $R_Q = \rho_Q L_Q/A_Q$.
Use the equal resistance condition $R_P = R_Q$, so $\rho_P L_P/A_P = \rho_Q L_Q/A_Q$.
Rearrange for the required length ratio: $L_P/L_Q = (\rho_Q/\rho_P) \times (A_P/A_Q)$.
Substitute the resistivity ratio $\rho_Q/\rho_P = 2$ and the area ratio from diameters: $d_Q = 2d_P$ gives $A_Q = 4A_P$, so $A_P/A_Q = 1/4$.
